analysis.one_liner: Caps fossil fuel emissions and pays every legal resident an equal quarterly dividend from the auction proceeds.
analysis.headline: The bill attracted 28 Democratic cosponsors but never received a committee markup or a floor vote, and it died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required oil refineries, coal mines, and natural gas suppliers to buy permits for the carbon dioxide their fuels release, with the number of permits shrinking every year until 2050, when emissions would be 80% below 2005 levels. All the auction money would have been sent back in equal quarterly payments to every person lawfully in the United States with a valid Social Security number. It also imposed fees on imports of carbon-intensive goods from countries without comparable climate rules, so U.S. factories would not be undercut. It never got a vote in committee or on the House floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Every person lawfully in the United States with a valid Social Security number would receive an equal quarterly share of the permit auction proceeds, tax-free. Because wealthy households and businesses burn far more energy than average, most low- and middle-income households would receive more in dividends than they pay in higher fuel and electricity prices. Renewable energy and carbon-capture industries would gain a growing market, and domestic manufacturers of steel, cement, and chemicals would be shielded from foreign competition by border fees.

how_it_helps.text: The bill sends 100% of the carbon permit auction proceeds and noncompliance penalties to a Healthy Climate Trust Fund, which pays an equal, tax-free quarterly dividend to every eligible individual, with an opt-out available [S3].
The permit cap declines on a fixed schedule from 12.5% below 2005 emissions in 2017 to 80% below by 2050, steadily cutting the pollution driving extreme weather and warming [S2][S3].

Fees on carbon-intensive imports (iron, steel, aluminum, cement, glass, paper, chemicals) and payments to U.S. exporters are designed to keep domestic manufacturers competitive against producers in countries without equivalent climate rules [S3].

Auction rules include limits on how many permits a single entity can buy or hold to prevent speculation and hoarding, and permit prices get a stabilization mechanism so households do not face wild price swings [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil refineries, petroleum importers, coal mines, and natural gas suppliers would pay for permits for every ton of carbon dioxide their fuels emit, with costs rising as the cap tightens. Those costs would be passed through to consumers in higher gasoline, heating, and electricity prices, hitting hardest the households and businesses that burn the most fuel. Coal-dependent mining regions would face the steepest pressure as their product became the most expensive to sell.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and heavy energy users

drawbacks.text: Gasoline, heating fuel, and electricity prices would rise before and alongside the dividends, and families who use unusually large amounts of energy — rural drivers, homes with high heating needs — would see the biggest upfront cost increases [S2][S3].
Coal-producing regions and communities built around mining would face economic contraction as their product became the most heavily taxed fuel under the cap [S2].

The dividend depends on individuals having a valid Social Security number and lawful presence, verified through tax and Social Security records, so people without that status would pay higher energy prices but receive nothing [S3].

A fixed annual cap cannot respond quickly to sudden energy price spikes, and while the bill borrows future permits to stabilize prices, doing so shifts allowable emissions into later years rather than eliminating them [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most households the math works in their favor: an equal per-person dividend usually exceeds what a low- or middle-income family pays in added fuel costs, and the long-term climate benefit — fewer heat waves, storms, floods, and fires — accrues to everyone. The genuine costs fall on fossil fuel producers, on coal-dependent towns, and on the heaviest energy users, and the bill does little for people excluded from the dividend while still paying higher prices. It was a substantial wealth transfer from fossil fuel extraction to the general public, which is precisely the design choice that made it hard to move in a Congress where the affected industries had strong allies.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred the bill to two committees the day it was introduced; the Energy and Commerce Committee sent it to its Energy and Power Subcommittee, and no markup, hearing record, or vote ever followed, so it expired when the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 24, 2015, by Rep. Chris Van Hollen with 16 original cosponsors, and was referred the same day to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee [S1][S5].

Six days later, on February 27, 2015, the Energy and Commerce Committee referred it to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power; the bill saw no further committee action for the remainder of the Congress [S5].
All 28 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican cosponsor is listed, and the bill never reached the House floor for any vote [S4][S5].
The bill expired on January 3, 2017, when the 114th Congress ended, without a committee markup or floor vote [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers avoided a rising carbon permit cost and coal producers avoided the steepest hit of all, because the bill never advanced far enough to threaten a vote. Households that would have received net dividends — most low- and middle-income families — gained nothing from the outcome.

sides.party_line_note: All 28 cosponsors were Democrats and the sponsor was a Democrat; the Republican-controlled House never scheduled the bill for any committee or floor action.

industries.note: Coal mines and coal importers would have to buy permits for every ton of carbon dioxide their fuel emits, and coal is the most carbon-intensive covered fuel, so the declining cap hits it hardest. The industry's interest in stopping the bill ran against the public dividend that would have been funded by those permit purchases.

Refineries and petroleum importers would pay permit costs on every barrel, costs that would be passed to consumers at the pump. Because the revenue returns to households, most ordinary people would come out ahead, which is why the industry's interest sat opposite the public's.

Gas suppliers and processors face the same permit obligation; gas is the least carbon-intensive covered fuel, so it would bear proportionally less cost than coal or oil while still funding the dividend.

industries.industry: Domestic heavy manufacturers (steel, cement, aluminum, glass, paper, chemicals)
industries.note: These producers would face higher energy costs under the cap, but the border adjustment charges equivalent fees on carbon-intensive imports and pays U.S. exporters, so they would not be undercut by competitors in countries without climate rules. Their interest in that protection runs alongside the public's.

A steadily shrinking fossil fuel permit cap creates a growing market for zero- and low-carbon alternatives, and the bill pays carbon permits for verifiable carbon capture and sequestration. The industry's growth depends on the same emissions reductions the public would benefit from.
